text.p: The following are the main stories from Wednesday morning's German newspapers:
FRANKFURTER ALLGEMEINE ZEITUNG
- More and more members of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU/CSU) want him to make a quick decision on whether he will run for reelection.
- Leaders of opposition Greens reject any notion of possible coalition with Christian Democrats.
- East German utilty companies say they are being overcharged by their suppliers.
- Wholesalers report week demand last year, decrease in turnover.
HANDELSBLATT
- Fraud in public construction contracts costs Germany at least five billion marks every year, expert estimates.
- Finance Minister Theo Waigel sticks to his projections for 1997, despute reports budget deficit set to rise above Maastricht limit.
- Government wants trade unions to change their negotiationg strategy in face of record unemployment.
SUEDDEUTSCHE ZEITUNG
- Oskar Lafontaine, leader of opposition Social Democrats (SPD), wants top rate of income tax to remain at 53 percent.
- State of Bavaria plans to slaughter 2,370 cattle imported from Britain and Switzerland in fight against mad cow disease.
- Savings banks warn they don't want European economic and monetary union to create huge market for big commercial banks.
- Chemicals sector banks on exports for boost in 1997, expects growth.
DIE WELT
- Leader of Free Democrats (FDP) expects Kohl to stand for reelection in 1998.
- Australia expresses interest in Transrapid magnetic railway project.
- Finance Ministry says it has not yet decided whether to impose a freeze on discretionary spending by government departments.
